title: Web Performance Optimization
tagline: Core Web Vitals (LCP, CLS, INP), bundling and code-splitting, lazy loading, HTTP caching strategies, CDN architecture, and the practical techniques that make pages fast.

sections.content:
Speed is not a luxury feature — it is the product itself. Studies consistently show that a 100ms delay in page load time can reduce conversion rates by 1%, and that 53% of mobile users abandon a site if it takes more than 3 seconds to load. Amazon calculated that each 100ms of additional latency cost them 1% in sales. Google has incorporated page speed into its search ranking algorithm since 2010, and the more recent **Core Web Vitals** initiative makes that relationship even more direct: pages that fail these metrics are penalised in rankings. Performance is therefore simultaneously a user experience problem, a business problem, and an SEO problem.

The challenge is that web performance is genuinely multi-dimensional. There is no single knob to turn. A page that downloads in 1 second can still feel sluggish if the layout jumps around as fonts and images load, or if it freezes for half a second when the user taps a button. A page with a tiny JavaScript bundle can still score poorly on LCP if the server takes 2 seconds to respond. This is why Google's Core Web Vitals decompose performance into three distinct, measurable, user-centric signals: **LCP** (did the main content arrive quickly?), **CLS** (did the page stay visually stable?), and **INP** (does the page respond to interactions promptly?).

But measuring performance is only the first layer. Making a page faster requires a layered toolkit: delivering less code (tree-shaking, minification, code-splitting), deferring non-critical work (lazy loading, async scripts), reusing prior responses (HTTP caching, service workers), and moving assets physically closer to users (CDNs, edge caching). This chapter covers the complete picture — from understanding the metrics and what drives them, through the build-time and runtime optimisation techniques, to caching and delivery architecture. By the end you will be able to diagnose a slow page, identify its bottlenecks, and apply targeted fixes.

sections.title: Web Performance as a Restaurant Kitchen
sections.content:
Think of a web page as a restaurant meal, and the browser as a diner who has just sat down:

**LCP** is when the main course arrives at the table — the most important, visible content the user came for. A good restaurant gets the main course out within 2.5 minutes of seating. If the diner is staring at an empty table for 4 minutes, they get anxious and may leave.

**CLS** is a clumsy waiter who keeps rearranging items on the table as you reach for them. You pick up your fork, and the plate suddenly slides 10cm to the left because the bread basket arrived and the waiter shoved things around. Every unexpected layout shift is that jarring rearrangement — your eyes and hands had planned for one position, and the page betrayed them.

**INP** is how quickly the waiter responds when you wave for attention. You push the call button, and 300ms later they acknowledge you and start moving. A 50ms waiter feels instantaneous; a 500ms waiter feels unresponsive.

Optimisation strategies map to restaurant improvements: **bundling and minification** means using smaller serving dishes (less to carry from kitchen to table, faster delivery). **Code splitting** means serving courses progressively — appetiser first, main course when ready — instead of trying to carry everything at once and dropping it at the door. **CDN** is opening branches closer to your customers so travel time is short. **HTTP caching** is a waiter who remembers a regular: 'You always order the salmon — I pre-prepared it while you were parking.' **Lazy loading** is not printing the dessert menu until someone actually asks to see it — why carry it to every table if most people leave after the main course?

sections.title: Core Web Vitals: The Three Signals That Define Perceived Performance
sections.content:
Google introduced Core Web Vitals in 2020 as a standardised, user-centric framework for measuring page experience. Unlike synthetic metrics such as DOMContentLoaded, Core Web Vitals capture what users actually perceive. There are three:

**LCP — Largest Contentful Paint** measures when the largest visible content element finishes rendering. Typically this is a hero image, an `<h1>` heading, or a large block of text. The browser continuously evaluates which element is the largest in the viewport and reports the time of its final render. The threshold for 'Good' is under **2.5 seconds** from navigation start; 'Needs Improvement' is 2.5–4s; 'Poor' is above 4s.

Common LCP killers include: high Time to First Byte (slow server), render-blocking scripts and stylesheets that delay the browser's painting phase, large unoptimised hero images (no compression, wrong format, no preload), and web fonts that delay text rendering (FOIT — flash of invisible text).

**CLS — Cumulative Layout Shift** is a dimensionless score that accumulates the visual impact of all unexpected layout shifts during the page's lifetime. Each shift is scored as `impact fraction × distance fraction` — how much of the viewport moved, and how far it moved. A score of 0 is perfect (nothing moved). 'Good' is under **0.1**; 'Needs Improvement' is 0.1–0.25; 'Poor' is above 0.25.

CLS is caused by: images and videos without explicit `width` and `height` attributes (the browser reserves no space, then shifts when dimensions become known), ads or embeds injecting content above existing DOM nodes, web fonts with `font-display: auto` causing FOUT (flash of unstyled text) or FOIT, and dynamically inserted banners or cookie notices that push content down.

**INP — Interaction to Next Paint** replaced FID (First Input Delay) as a Core Web Vital in March 2024. FID only measured the delay before the browser could begin handling the *first* interaction. INP is more comprehensive: it measures the **worst-case latency** of every click, tap, and keypress over the entire page lifetime and reports that worst case as the page's INP score. The threshold for 'Good' is under **200ms**; 'Needs Improvement' is 200–500ms; 'Poor' is above 500ms.

INP is caused by long tasks blocking the main thread (JavaScript that runs for more than 50ms without yielding), heavy event handlers that perform synchronous DOM reads then writes (forced layout / layout thrashing), non-yielding computational loops, and third-party scripts that hog the main thread.

sections.title: Measuring Performance: Lighthouse, CrUX, and PerformanceObserver
sections.content:
There are three complementary ways to measure Core Web Vitals:

**Lighthouse** is a synthetic audit tool built into Chrome DevTools (and available as a CLI, Node API, or via PageSpeed Insights). It simulates page load under throttled network and CPU conditions, producing a scored report with specific recommendations. Because it runs in a controlled environment, it is ideal for CI/CD gates — you can fail a build if LCP rises above a threshold. The score is deterministic and reproducible.

**CrUX (Chrome User Experience Report)** is Google's dataset of real-world performance data collected from opt-in Chrome users. When you test a URL on PageSpeed Insights (pagespeed.web.dev), the 'Field Data' section shows CrUX metrics for your actual visitors — their real devices, connections, and geographic distribution. CrUX data is what Google uses for search ranking, making it the ground truth that matters. A page can score 95 in Lighthouse but fail CWV in CrUX if real users have slower devices.

**PerformanceObserver** is the browser API that lets you measure Core Web Vitals from JavaScript running in the page itself. This is what the `web-vitals` npm library wraps. It uses entry types like `'largest-contentful-paint'`, `'layout-shift'`, and `'event'` to collect raw measurements, which you can then send to your analytics pipeline. This gives you RUM (Real User Monitoring) — field data from your own users without relying on Google's dataset.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: `PerformanceObserver` gives you raw access to Core Web Vitals measurements from within the page. The key subtleties: LCP fires multiple times as larger elements are discovered, so always use the last entry. CLS must filter entries with `hadRecentInput` (user scrolls or zooms are intentional, not unexpected shifts). For production, the `web-vitals` library from Google handles these edge cases correctly and is the recommended approach.

sections.title: The Critical Rendering Path: Why Some Resources Block Paint
sections.content:
Understanding why pages are slow requires understanding the **critical rendering path** — the sequence of steps the browser must complete before it can paint anything on screen:

1. **Parse HTML** → build the DOM (Document Object Model)
2. **Parse CSS** → build the CSSOM (CSS Object Model)
3. **Combine DOM + CSSOM** → build the Render Tree
4. **Layout** → calculate position and size of every element
5. **Paint** → fill in pixels on layers
6. **Composite** → combine layers into the final screen image

CSS is **render-blocking**: the browser cannot build the Render Tree without the CSSOM, so it cannot paint until all CSS in `<link rel='stylesheet'>` tags has been downloaded and parsed. A large CSS file or a stylesheet hosted on a slow server delays every pixel on the page.

JavaScript (by default) is **parser-blocking AND render-blocking**: when the parser encounters a `<script>` tag, it stops parsing HTML, downloads the script, and executes it (because the script might call `document.write()` or modify the DOM). Only then does parsing resume. This is why the golden rule for classic scripts is to place them at the bottom of `<body>` — at that point the DOM is already parsed.

Modern mitigation attributes: `defer` downloads the script in parallel with HTML parsing and executes it after parsing completes (in document order). `async` downloads in parallel and executes as soon as it arrives, potentially interrupting parsing. Use `defer` for scripts that depend on the DOM; use `async` for truly independent analytics scripts.

For CSS, the main mitigations are: inline critical CSS (the styles needed for above-the-fold content) directly in `<style>` tags in the `<head>`, and load non-critical CSS asynchronously. This eliminates the render-blocking delay for initial paint while still delivering full styles before the user sees below-the-fold content.

    Server-->>Browser: HTML

sections.title: JavaScript Bundling, Tree-Shaking, and Minification
sections.content:
Modern web applications are written in hundreds or thousands of JavaScript files using ES module `import`/`export` syntax. The browser cannot efficiently download 500 individual small files (each HTTP request has overhead), so **bundlers** — Vite, webpack, esbuild, Rollup — combine them into fewer, larger files.

But bundling alone can produce enormous files if the developer is not careful. Three build-time techniques keep bundle sizes manageable:

**Tree-shaking** (dead code elimination) is the process of statically analysing the import graph and removing exports that are never actually imported anywhere. It requires **ES modules** (the `import`/`export` syntax) because ES modules have static, analysable structure. CommonJS (`require()`) is dynamic — you can compute the module name at runtime — so bundlers cannot determine what is actually used.

The classic anti-pattern: `import _ from 'lodash'` pulls the entire lodash library (over 500KB uncompressed) into your bundle even if you only need `debounce`. The fix: `import { debounce } from 'lodash-es'` — lodash-es is the ES module version, and the bundler tree-shakes everything except `debounce`. This single change can reduce bundle size by 400–500KB.

**Minification** removes everything a computer does not need but a human finds readable: whitespace, comments, long variable names. `const maximumNumberOfRetries = 3` becomes `const a=3`. Minifiers like esbuild, terser, and swc also perform constant folding, dead code removal within functions, and inlining of small functions. A typical minified bundle is 30–60% smaller than the original.

**Compression** is the final layer. After minification, the server (or CDN) applies **Brotli** or gzip compression before transmitting the file. Brotli (designed by Google specifically for web assets) achieves roughly 20% better compression than gzip on typical JavaScript. The browser decompresses transparently. A 200KB minified bundle might compress to 60KB with Brotli. Always configure your CDN or server to serve `.js` files with `Content-Encoding: br` (Brotli) or `Content-Encoding: gzip`.

sections.title: Code Splitting: Loading Only What the Current Page Needs
sections.content:
Even with tree-shaking, a large single-page application can have hundreds of kilobytes of JavaScript for routes and features the user has never visited. **Code splitting** solves this by dividing the bundle into smaller **chunks** that are loaded on demand.

The mechanism is the dynamic `import()` expression — a proposal that became standard in ES2020. When a bundler encounters `import('./chart.js')`, it creates a separate chunk file for `chart.js` and all of its unique dependencies. That chunk is not included in the initial bundle; it is downloaded only when the `import()` call executes at runtime.

There are two main patterns for code splitting:

**Route-based splitting** is the most impactful. Each route in a SPA gets its own chunk. React Router with React.lazy, Vue Router with async components, and Next.js pages are all examples. A user visiting the dashboard never downloads the code for the settings page, the admin panel, or the reports section. For large apps, this can reduce the initial load from 800KB to 80KB.

**Component-level splitting** targets heavy components that are conditionally rendered. A rich text editor, a data grid, a PDF viewer — these can be tens of kilobytes of JavaScript. Wrapping them in `React.lazy(() => import('./RichEditor'))` means the code downloads only when the component is first rendered, not on initial page load.

A key concept: **chunk hashing**. Bundlers generate filenames like `chart.a1b2c3d4.js` where the hash is derived from the file's content. When the content changes (a new deploy), the hash changes, creating a new URL. This means you can safely set very long cache lifetimes on chunk files — browsers that have the old hash cached will never accidentally reuse stale JavaScript, because new deploys create new URLs.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: `React.lazy` wraps a dynamic `import()` — the bundler (Vite, webpack) detects this and splits the module into its own chunk file. `Suspense` provides the fallback UI while the chunk loads. For non-React code, a bare dynamic `import()` in an event handler achieves the same split. The proactive `preloadDashboard()` trick downloads the chunk silently while the user is still on the login page, making the subsequent navigation feel instant.

sections.title: Image Optimization: The Hidden Source of LCP and CLS Problems
sections.content: Images are typically the largest resources on any web page and are responsible for the majority of LCP and CLS issues. A comprehensive image strategy addresses format, sizing, lazy loading, and priority. **Modern formats**: JPEG and PNG are the legacy baseline. **WebP** (Google, 2010) achieves 25–34% smaller file sizes than JPEG at equivalent quality for photographs, and supports transparency. **AVIF** (AV1 Image Format, 2019) achieves a further 20% improvement over WebP but has slightly higher encoding cost. Use `` with `` and `` for progressive enhancement with a JPEG fallback. **Responsive images**: Use `srcset` and `sizes` to serve different image resolutions to different viewport widths. A mobile user with a 390px screen should not download a 1920px image. `srcset='hero-400.webp 400w, hero-800.webp 800w, hero-1600.webp 1600w'` tells the browser what sizes are available; `sizes='(max-width: 768px) 100vw, 50vw'` tells it how wide the image will be on screen. **Explicit dimensions prevent CLS**: Without `width` and `height` attributes, the browser allocates zero space for an image in the layout. When the image loads and its dimensions become known, the browser recalculates layout — everything below the image shifts down. This is the single most common CLS cause. Setting `width='800' height='600'` gives the browser the aspect ratio (800/600 = 4:3) so it reserves the right amount of space before the image downloads. **Lazy loading for below-fold images**: `loading='lazy'` on `` tells the browser to defer downloading images until they are near the viewport. This reduces initial page weight and bandwidth, speeding up LCP (fewer bytes competing for the network). Critical: **never** use `loading='lazy'` on the LCP image itself — it delays the most important content. **Priority for the LCP image**: Add `fetchpriority='high'` to the LCP image element. This moves it to the top of the browser's network request queue. For images discovered in CSS (background-image) or injected by JavaScript, you need a `` tag in the `` to ensure early discovery.

sections.title: HTTP Caching: Making Repeat Visits Free
sections.content:
HTTP caching allows the browser (and CDN) to store responses and reuse them without making network requests. Properly configured caching makes repeat visits nearly instantaneous and dramatically reduces origin server load.

The key header is **`Cache-Control`**, introduced in HTTP/1.1. Its directives work together:

`max-age=N` tells the browser to consider the cached response fresh for N seconds. Within the freshness window, the browser serves from cache without any network request at all.

`immutable` (a newer directive) tells the browser that this resource will never change at this URL, so it should not revalidate even when the user does a hard refresh. Combined with content-hashed filenames, this is the gold standard for static assets.

`no-cache` does NOT mean 'do not cache' — it means 'cache it, but revalidate before using it'. The browser stores the response, and on subsequent requests sends a conditional request with `If-None-Match` (ETag) or `If-Modified-Since`. If unchanged, the server returns `304 Not Modified` with no body — much faster than re-sending the full resource, but still a network round trip.

`no-store` means genuinely do not cache — never store a copy. Use for sensitive responses (banking, medical data, session information).

The **optimal strategy** depends on whether the URL can change:

**Content-hashed assets** (`app.a1b2c3.js`, `styles.8f4d2e.css`): The hash in the filename changes with every deploy. Set `Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable` (1 year). Browsers cache indefinitely; old hashes are never requested again after a new deploy creates new filenames.

**The HTML document** (`index.html`): This must always be fresh, because it contains the references to the current chunk filenames. Set `Cache-Control: no-cache` (or `max-age=0, must-revalidate`). The browser revalidates on every load but uses the cached copy if unchanged (304).

**API responses**: Typically `no-store` for user-specific data. Short `max-age` (30–300s) for shared, slowly-changing data like product catalogues.

sections.title: CDN Architecture: Bringing Content Closer to Users
sections.content:
A **Content Delivery Network** is a geographically distributed network of proxy servers called **edge nodes** or **Points of Presence (PoPs)**. When a user requests a static asset, DNS resolves the CDN domain to the geographically nearest edge node. The edge serves a cached copy of the asset if available; on a cache miss, it fetches from the origin server, caches the response, and serves it.

The performance benefit is primarily about **latency**, not bandwidth. Network round-trip time (RTT) is limited by the speed of light. A request from Tokyo to a New York origin server travels approximately 11,000km each way — at the speed of light in fiber (about 200,000 km/s), that is 55ms one-way, or 110ms RTT for a single round trip. Serving from a Tokyo edge server reduces this to 5–10ms. For a page that requires 5–10 sequential round trips to load all its assets, this difference compounds dramatically.

CDNs provide additional benefits: **TLS termination** at the edge (the expensive TLS handshake happens close to the user), **HTTP/2 and HTTP/3** support even if the origin only speaks HTTP/1.1, **automatic Brotli/gzip compression**, **DDoS mitigation** (the distributed network absorbs attack traffic), and **origin shielding** (a special edge node sits in front of the origin to reduce the number of cache-miss fetches that reach origin).

**Cache invalidation at the CDN** is the hard problem. When you deploy new code, how do you ensure edge nodes serve the new version? Content-hashed filenames solve this elegantly for static assets — new filenames mean new cache keys, no invalidation needed. For the HTML document and API responses, you use cache headers with short TTLs, or trigger explicit cache purges via the CDN's API. Major CDNs (Cloudflare, Fastly, CloudFront) support tagged purging: you tag cached responses and purge by tag on deploy.

**Edge computing** is the next evolution: running code (not just caching) at CDN edge nodes. Cloudflare Workers, Fastly Compute, and Vercel Edge Functions let you personalise responses, run A/B tests, and modify headers at the edge without going back to origin. This further reduces latency for dynamic content.

sections.explanation: The Cache-Control regex matches content-hashed filenames (8+ hex characters before the extension) to apply immutable caching only to those assets. The hero image configuration shows every performance attribute working together: `width`/`height` prevent CLS, `fetchPriority='high'` improves LCP, and `decoding='async'` keeps the main thread free. The chunked processing pattern is the core technique for breaking up long tasks to improve INP — `setTimeout(resolve, 0)` yields to the event loop, allowing the browser to process pending user interactions between chunks.

sections.title: INP and Main Thread Management: Keeping the Page Responsive
sections.content:
INP is the newest Core Web Vital and the one most developers find hardest to fix, because it requires understanding how the browser's event loop works.

The browser runs JavaScript on a single **main thread**. This thread is also responsible for processing user input events, running CSS animations, painting pixels, and handling garbage collection. When JavaScript runs a long task — anything taking more than 50ms — the browser cannot process input events until that task completes. This creates the visible 'jank' or 'freeze' that INP measures.

**Identifying long tasks**: Chrome DevTools Performance panel highlights tasks longer than 50ms in red. The `PerformanceObserver` with `type: 'longtask'` lets you detect them programmatically. The Lighthouse report's 'Total Blocking Time' (TBT) metric correlates strongly with INP.

**Breaking up long tasks**: The key technique is **yielding** — voluntarily returning control to the event loop at intervals so the browser can handle pending inputs. The classic approach is `setTimeout(fn, 0)`, which schedules the next chunk in a new macrotask. The newer **Scheduler API** (`scheduler.postTask()`) gives more control over task priority.

**Web Workers** move computation entirely off the main thread. If you need to parse a large JSON file, run a search algorithm, or perform image processing, a Web Worker does the work on a background thread without blocking input events. Communication between main thread and worker uses `postMessage` and is asynchronous. The limitation: workers cannot access the DOM directly.

**Event handler hygiene**: Avoid **forced synchronous layout** (also called layout thrashing) inside event handlers. Reading a layout property (`offsetHeight`, `getBoundingClientRect()`) after a DOM write forces the browser to synchronously recalculate layout before returning the value. In a loop, this can turn a 5ms operation into a 500ms freeze. The fix: batch reads first, then writes.

**Debouncing and throttling**: For continuous input events like `scroll`, `resize`, `input`, and `mousemove`, the event fires dozens of times per second. Running an expensive handler on every fire is wasteful. Debounce waits until the user pauses (runs once after a gap); throttle runs at most once per interval.

**A brief history of web performance metrics**: Before Core Web Vitals, developers relied on synthetic metrics like DOMContentLoaded (when HTML is parsed) and `load` (when all resources finish). These correlated poorly with user perception — a page could fire `load` in 2s but feel slow because the main content appeared at 4s. Google's internal research found that **user satisfaction** correlates best with: how quickly the main content appears (LCP), whether content jumps around (CLS), and whether the page responds to input (INP). These three signals, chosen because they directly mirror human perception, became the Core Web Vitals in 2020. FID (First Input Delay) was the original interactivity metric but was replaced by INP in March 2024 because FID only measured the *first* interaction — a page could have great FID but terrible responsiveness for subsequent interactions.

**Start with measurement, not guesses. Then target the highest-ROI fixes first.** Run Lighthouse in Chrome DevTools (or PageSpeed Insights) to get a scored report with specific, prioritised recommendations. Check PageSpeed Insights for field data from real users — your Lighthouse score and your CrUX data may differ significantly. The three highest-ROI improvements for most apps: (1) set explicit `width` and `height` on every `` — eliminates CLS, zero code complexity; (2) add `fetchpriority='high'` to the LCP image and ensure it is in HTML (not injected by JS) — improves LCP; (3) code-split your bundle by route — can reduce initial JS by 60–80% on large apps. Common interview trap: `loading='lazy'` on the LCP image actively *hurts* performance by deprioritising the most important content. Always `fetchpriority='high'` on LCP, `loading='lazy'` on everything else below the fold.

items: **Core Web Vitals** are Google's user-centric metrics: LCP (main content visible, target <2.5s), CLS (visual stability, target <0.1), and INP (worst-case interaction latency, target <200ms). They directly affect search ranking and user experience.

**The critical rendering path** explains why performance matters at the HTML level: CSS is render-blocking, synchronous scripts are parser-blocking. Use `defer` for DOM-dependent scripts, inline critical CSS, and `<link rel=preload>` for LCP images to minimise the delay before first paint.

**Code splitting** with dynamic `import()` prevents loading JavaScript for unvisited routes or features. Bundlers create separate chunk files; combined with content-hashed filenames and `Cache-Control: immutable`, this gives both small initial bundles and optimal caching.

**Tree-shaking** requires ES modules (`import`/`export`) and named imports. Never `import _ from 'lodash'` — always `import { debounce } from 'lodash-es'`. A single such change can remove hundreds of kilobytes from a bundle.

**Images dominate both LCP and CLS**: use `fetchpriority='high'` on the LCP image (never `loading='lazy'`), set explicit `width` and `height` on every image, use `loading='lazy'` for below-fold images, and serve AVIF or WebP formats with `<picture>` for progressive enhancement.

**HTTP caching strategy is URL-driven**: content-hashed assets get `max-age=31536000, immutable` (cached forever, new deploy = new URL); the HTML document gets `no-cache` (revalidated every load via ETag); sensitive API data gets `no-store`.

**CDNs reduce latency** by serving from edge nodes near users. The performance benefit compounds across multiple round trips. Pair with content-hashed filenames so cache invalidation is implicit (new hash = new URL) rather than requiring explicit purges.

quiz.question: What does LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) specifically measure?
options: The time until the very first pixel is painted on screen
When the largest visible content element (image or text block) finishes rendering
The total number of layout shifts accumulated during page load
How quickly the browser responds to the first user interaction
quiz.explanation: LCP measures when the largest element visible in the viewport — typically a hero image, H1 heading, or large text block — finishes rendering. Good LCP is under 2.5s from navigation start. FCP (First Contentful Paint) measures the first pixel; CLS measures layout shifts; INP measures interaction latency.

quiz.question: A page has a hero image without `width` and `height` attributes. Which Core Web Vital does this most directly harm?
options: LCP, because the image is larger without explicit dimensions
INP, because the browser must compute layout on interaction
CLS, because the browser cannot reserve space before the image loads
TTFB, because the server takes longer to respond
quiz.explanation: Without explicit width/height, the browser allocates zero space for the image in the layout. When the image loads and its dimensions become known, the browser recalculates layout, shifting all content below the image — this is a layout shift scored by CLS. Setting width and height gives the browser the aspect ratio to reserve the correct space before the download completes.

quiz.question: What is tree-shaking and why does it require ES modules (`import`/`export`)?
options: Removing unused CSS; CSS has static structure that can be analysed at build time
Eliminating unused JavaScript exports at build time; ES modules have static import structure that bundlers can analyse
Splitting bundles into chunks; ES modules support async loading unlike CommonJS
Compressing assets with Brotli; ES module syntax enables better compression ratios
quiz.explanation: Tree-shaking (dead code elimination) removes exports that are never imported anywhere in the application. It requires ES modules because their import/export statements are static and analysable at build time — the bundler can definitively determine what is and is not used. CommonJS `require()` is dynamic (you can compute the module name at runtime), so bundlers cannot safely remove anything.

quiz.question: What does `import('./chart.js')` (dynamic import) cause a module bundler like Vite or webpack to do?
options: Run chart.js in a Web Worker to avoid blocking the main thread
Import only the default export from chart.js, tree-shaking named exports
Create a separate bundle chunk for chart.js that is downloaded only when the import() executes
Inline chart.js directly into the main bundle with tree-shaking applied
quiz.explanation: Dynamic `import()` is the code-splitting point for bundlers. When encountered, the bundler creates a separate chunk file containing chart.js and its unique dependencies. This chunk is not included in the initial bundle — it is a separate file downloaded only when the `import()` call executes at runtime. This keeps initial bundle size small.

quiz.question: Which `Cache-Control` header should be set for a content-hashed JavaScript file like `app.a1b2c3d4.js`?
options: no-store
no-cache
max-age=3600, public
max-age=31536000, immutable
quiz.explanation: Content-hashed assets have unique URLs that change when the content changes (new deploy = new hash = new URL). They should be cached for as long as possible — one year (31,536,000 seconds) — with `immutable` telling browsers to never revalidate. When a new version is deployed, the hash changes, creating a new URL that is not in any browser cache. Old cached files are simply never requested again.

quiz.question: INP (Interaction to Next Paint) replaced FID (First Input Delay) as a Core Web Vital in March 2024. What was the main weakness of FID that INP addresses?
options: FID measured paint time rather than input processing time
FID only measured the delay before the very first interaction; INP measures the worst-case latency across all interactions
FID required a user to interact before it could be measured; INP works on pages with no interactions
FID was only available in Chrome; INP works across all browsers
quiz.explanation: FID measured the delay between the user's first interaction and when the browser could begin processing it — but only the first interaction. A page could have excellent FID (the first click was fast) but terrible responsiveness for all subsequent interactions. INP measures the worst-case latency across ALL clicks, taps, and keypresses during the entire page lifetime, providing a more complete picture of interactivity.

quiz.question: A developer writes `import _ from 'lodash'` and uses only `_.debounce`. What is the performance problem?
options: lodash uses CommonJS and cannot be used with async/await
The entire lodash library (500KB+) is included in the bundle because bundlers cannot tree-shake CommonJS default imports
Dynamic imports are required for lodash to work in modern browsers
lodash default import bypasses the browser cache on repeated visits
quiz.explanation: Importing the lodash default export includes all 600+ utilities in the bundle — the bundler cannot determine which parts are unused because lodash uses CommonJS format, which is dynamic. The fix: use `import { debounce } from 'lodash-es'` (the ES module version). The bundler can then statically analyse that only `debounce` is used and tree-shake everything else, potentially saving 400-500KB.

quiz.question: What is the primary mechanism by which a CDN reduces page load time for geographically distant users?
options: It compresses assets more aggressively than origin servers can
It eliminates the need for TLS, reducing connection overhead
It serves cached assets from edge nodes near the user, reducing network round-trip latency
It batches multiple HTTP requests into a single TCP connection
quiz.explanation: A CDN's primary benefit is geographic distribution — edge servers near users serve cached assets with short network round-trip times. A user in Tokyo fetching from a New York origin faces ~110ms RTT per round trip; fetching from a Tokyo edge node reduces this to ~10ms. This latency reduction compounds across multiple resources. Compression, HTTP/2, and TLS termination are secondary benefits.

quiz.question: CSS stylesheets loaded with `<link rel='stylesheet'>` are described as 'render-blocking'. What does this mean?
options: The browser stops downloading other resources until the CSS finishes loading
The browser cannot build the Render Tree (and thus cannot paint) until the CSS is downloaded and parsed
JavaScript cannot execute until the CSS is fully applied to the DOM
The CSS file prevents the HTML parser from building the DOM
quiz.explanation: CSS is render-blocking because the browser needs the complete CSSOM (built from CSS) to construct the Render Tree, which is required before any painting can occur. If a CSS file is slow to download, the browser has a complete DOM but cannot paint anything — the page stays blank. This is why inline critical CSS (for above-the-fold content) eliminates the render-blocking delay for initial paint.

quiz.question: A long JavaScript loop (300ms) runs in a click event handler, causing the page to freeze. Which technique best fixes this without moving work off the main thread?
options: Wrap the loop in requestAnimationFrame to synchronise with the display refresh rate
Move the loop into a Promise chain so it runs asynchronously
Split the loop into chunks and yield to the event loop between chunks using setTimeout or scheduler.postTask
Use a Service Worker to intercept and cache the computation result
quiz.explanation: The browser's main thread processes both JavaScript and user input. A 300ms synchronous loop blocks input processing for its entire duration. Splitting the loop into chunks (e.g., 50 items at a time) and yielding between chunks with `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 0))` returns control to the event loop so the browser can process any pending interactions between chunks. This reduces the worst-case INP from 300ms to near-zero. Promises and rAF do not yield to the macrotask queue in the way needed.
